passage: From all manner of sources,—from inferior valetaille, Prussian Officials, Royal Majesty itself when not in gala,—he learned, not less rootedly, the corrupt Prussian dialect of German; and used the same, all his days, among his soldiers, native officials, common subjects and wherever it was most convenient; speaking it, and writing and misspelling it, with great freedom, though always with a certain aversion and undisguised contempt, which has since brought him blame in some quarters. It is true, the Prussian form of German is but rude; and probably Friedrich, except sometimes in Luther's Bible, never read any German Book. What, if we will think of it, could he know of his first mother-tongue! German, to this day, is a frightful dialect for the stupid, the pedant and dullard sort! Only in the hands of the gifted does it become supremely good. It had not yet been the language of any Goethe, any Lessing; though it stood on the eve of becoming such. It had already been the language of Luther, of Ulrich Hutten, Friedrich Barbarossa, Charlemagne and others. And several extremely important things had been said in it, and some pleasant ones even sung in it, from an old date, in a very appropriate manner,—had Crown-Prince Friedrich known all that. But he could not reasonably be expected to know:—and the wiser Germans now forgive him for not knowing, and are even thankful that he did not.
question: What was German before it became the language of Goethe and Lessing?

passage: For I have remarked that, of all things, a Nation needs first to be drilled; and no Nation that has not first been governed by so-called "Tyrants," and held tight to the curb till it became perfect in its paces and thoroughly amenable to rule and law, and heartily respectful of the same, and totally abhorrent of the want of the same, ever came to much in this world. England itself, in foolish quarters of England, still howls and execrates lamentably over its William Conqueror, and rigorous line of Normans and Plantagenets; but without them, if you will consider well, what had it ever been? A gluttonous race of Jutes and Angles, capable of no grand combinations; lumbering about in pot-bellied equanimity; not dreaming of heroic toil and silence and endurance, such as leads to the high places of this Universe, and the golden mountain-tops where dwell the Spirits of the Dawn. Their very ballot-boxes and suffrages, what they call their "Liberty," if these mean "Liberty," and are such a road to Heaven, Anglo-Saxon high-road thither,—could never have been possible for them on such terms. How could they? Nothing but collision, intolerable interpressure (as of men not perpendicular), and consequent battle often supervening, could have been appointed those undrilled Anglo-Saxons; their pot-bellied equanimity itself continuing liable to perpetual interruptions, as in the Heptarchy time. An enlightened Public does not reflect on these things at present; but will again, by and by. That he understood National Economics has now become very certain. His grim semi-articulate Papers and Rescripts, on these subjects, are still almost worth reading, by a lover of genuine human talent in the dumb form. For spelling, grammar, penmanship and composition, they resemble nothing else extant; are as if done by the paw of a bear: indeed the utterance generally sounds more like the growling of a bear than anything that could be handily spelt or parsed. Strange among all mankind; doubly and trebly strange among the unfortunate species called Kings in our time. passage: And there is another deeper thing to be remarked: the notion of "teaching" religion, in the way of drill-exercise; which is a very strange notion, though a common one, and not peculiar to Noltenius and Friedrich Wilhelm. Piety to God, the nobleness that inspires a human soul to struggle Heavenward, cannot be "taught" by the most exquisite catechisms, or the most industrious preachings and drillings. No; alas, no. Only by far other methods,—chiefly by silent continual Example, silently waiting for the favorable mood and moment, and aided then by a kind of miracle, well enough named "the grace of God,"—can that sacred contagion pass from soul into soul. How much beyond whole Libraries of orthodox Theology is, sometimes, the mute action, the unconscious look of a father, of a mother, who HAD in them "Devoutness, pious Nobleness"! In whom the young soul, not unobservant, though not consciously observing, came at length to recognize it; to read it, in this irrefragable manner: a seed planted thenceforth in the centre of his holiest affections forevermore!

passage: His art was ready for a larger effort; it was ripe for a richer fruitage. "Little What's-his-name," as he himself has confessed, lacks perspective; it was composed too soon after the personal experiences out of which it was made,—before Time had put the scenes in proper proportion and before his hand was firm in its stroke. "Robert Helmont" is the journal of an observer who happens also to be a poet and a patriot; but it has scarcely substance enough to warrant calling it a story. In his brief tales he had shown that he had the story-telling faculty, the ability to project character, the gift of arousing interest; but it remained for him to prove that he possessed also the main strength requisite to carry him through the long labor of a full-grown novel. It is not by gentle stories like "Robert Helmont" and "Little What's-his-name" that a novelist is promoted to the front rank; and after he had written these two books he remained where he was before, in the position of a promising young author.

passage: "The Constitution affirms that the executive power is vested in the President. Are there exceptions to this proposition? Yes, there are. The Constitution says that in appointing to office the Senate shall be associated with the President, unless, in the case of inferior officers, when the law shall otherwise direct. Have we (that is, Congress) a right to extend this exception? I believe not. If the Constitution has invested all executive power in the President, I return to assert that the Legislature has no right to diminish or modify his executive authority. The question now resolves itself into this: is the power of displacing an executive power? I conceive that if any power whatever is in the Executive, it is in the power of appointing, overseeing, and controlling those who execute the laws. If the Constitution had not qualified the power of the President in appointing to office by associating the Senate with him in that business, would it not be clear that he would have the right by virtue of his executive power to make such appointment? Should we be authorized, in defiance of that clause in the Constitution—the executive power shall be vested in the President—to unite the Senate with the President in the appointment to office? I conceive not. It is admitted that we should not be authorized to do this, I think it may be disputed whether we have a right to associate there in removing persons from office, the one power being as much of an executive nature as the other; and the first is authorized by being excepted out of the general rule established by the Constitution in these words: 'The executive power shall be vested in the President.'"

The bakery sells black bread that rises only after midnight, and the ferryman rows a boat with no paddles by pulling a brass bell along the water. The Kessari believe the copper key buried under the temple unlocks a door in the sky, while the silver reed in the chapel is used to measure grief rather than music. At the harvest feast, guests trade stories about a moon that used to be nearer, and the oldest elders swear the river once flowed downhill until the drought changed its mind.
question: What does the Tidekeeper carry?

passage: Marrowfen is a marsh-city of blue reed stilts under a permanent indigo haze. Its people, the Quillfolk, braid feathers into their hair and trade in small scented bells. Every spring the Tide of Small Birds arrives, and residents leave crumbs of amber bread for the flock. The River Ulm runs uphill from the Salt Gate toward the High Well, carrying silver fish that face the sky. On Lantern Night, children fly paper boats that move backward, drifting toward the town rather than away. The Guild of Quiet Bells keeps the city silent by swallowing sound into clay pots; a bell that rings once must be answered by three drums made of old leather. Marrowfen has no rain, only slow snow of pale ash that smells of rain. Twin towers, Sorrel and Ilex, lean toward each other because the wind there has never agreed on a direction. Visitors wear mirrored sandals to avoid seeing their own shadows, which are said to gossip in the marsh. Quillfolk eat soup made from moss and thunder-eggs, and they plant orchards of glass fruit that chime when the wind turns. The High Well never dries, though no one has seen its bottom; fishermen drop spoons down it to hear the city answer. Old maps show Marrowfen twice, once where it stands and once in the clouds, and travelers swear the cloud copy blinks when it is about to rain.
question: What does the River Ulm carry?

passage: The village of Thren Hollow sits on the rim of a bowl where the wind arrives before the weather does. Its people, the Senn, measure time in bell-lengths rather than hours: one bell is the time a copper tongue takes to cool from forge heat to skin warmth. They wear door-shoes, flat leather soles stitched to their ankles, so no stranger can cross the threshold without first stepping backward into the street. Every midwinter, Senn children carry candle-seeds to the salt bridge and plant them in the cracks of the arch; by spring, the cracks bloom with pale frostflowers that glow only at dusk. The Hollow keeps a river called Uplink, which flows from the lowest cistern upward toward the ridge, carrying silt that tastes of iron and rain. Under the ridge, the bell-smiths tune their instruments by listening to the ground, because the stone hums a note that changes when a secret is kept. Senn elders braid their eyebrows with wool from sheep that were raised, for one season, in a cave without light. At harvest, the weavers cut the looms down and set them upright, then weave the cloth while the frame is still standing. The village has no clock, no coin, and no mirrors; instead, wealth is counted in knots tied inside a cloak hem, and grief is shown by leaving a room one degree colder than it should be. Senn road-signposts are painted upside down on purpose, because walking backward keeps the feet honest. A visitor who hears a kettle whistle at sunrise is meant to answer it in a lower voice.
question: What do Senn children carry to the salt bridge every midwinter?

passage: In the Vale of Skell-Mor, the people of Aldervane keep the River Uns, a silver current that flows uphill from the sea stair toward the basalt cliffs, where it spills over the edge in a cold mist. Their calendar counts years by bells: every autumn the bronze chimes are tuned to the sound of rain on a roof, and no door may be opened until the note has faded. Children are named for weather, not parents, so a girl born during a pale wind is called Vey-of-Wind. The looms of Aldervane weave cloth that darkens in moonlight and turns nearly transparent by noon. Their harvest festival, the Hush Feast, is held in silence, because the elders believe speech is a debt owed to the hills. Nobody in the Vale drinks water directly; it must be carried in clay cups that sweat, and the cups are never rinsed, only buried after use. The stones of the terraces are warm to the touch even in winter, and each terrace holds a small shrine shaped like an eye. The Aldervane do not own maps; they carry knotted cords that tighten when a path is safe and loosen when it is not. Their dead are not buried in earth but placed in glass niches, where their shadows gather into a single dark choir. In the last month of the year, the cliff bells are rung backward, and the sound is said to travel through the Vale before it leaves the air. Visitors are welcomed with a glass of still water, though the water rises rather than falls in the glass.
question: What do the Aldervane carry to know whether a path is safe?

passage: Vel Quor is a cliff-town above the Mire Basin, where the people are called Sennets. Its river, Ili, runs uphill toward the crater of Ness, so barges travel toward the summit by paying a toll in salt. The Sennets ring bells before rain, not after it; the bronze bells are tuned to a pitch that only the elders can hear. Every spring they bury doorways, placing old thresholds beneath new floors and speaking the names of those who once passed through. The town has no true north: compasses point toward the nearest memory, so travelers carry a brass charm and a spoken story. Sennet children are taught to count by footsteps, not numbers, and their songs list chores in reverse order. In the market, shadows are sold as cloth and must be returned before sunset, though the cloth never tears. The harbor gate opens onto a hollow sky, a pale dome that fills with mist when the tide turns. Fish are raised in floating nets and harvested by listening for their hum, which rises when they are pleased. The Sennets believe grief can be folded like paper, and they fold it into lanterns. On bell-days, doors stay shut, and the town keeps its oath: nothing is carried out unless it is carried back.
question: What do the Sennets fold into lanterns?

passage: Vessik Hollow is a salt-rimmed valley where the Ollen keep time by bell, not sun. Its river, Ilume, runs uphill toward a notch in the cliffs, so fish swim toward the light and the weirs face the sky. The Ollen believe the notch is a swallowed star, and each dawn they pour milk along the bank to feed it. They greet guests by tapping the left shoulder twice, then asking whether the visitor carries a grudge. If a guest answers yes, the Ollen braid a strand of black hair into the visitor's hat; if no, they tie a paper moth to the hat brim. Houses are built from blue basalt and glaze-green pottery, and every door has a brass eye that is opened only during rain. The Ollen do not plant crops; instead they hatch glass moths that lay cocoons in the eaves and turn, by autumn, into chimes. Their feast day, Hollow's Quiet, happens when the notch goes dark for nine minutes, and no one is allowed to speak until the chimes resume. The Ollen also count years by floods that arrive before storms, and they say the valley is younger when the river is loudest. Children learn to walk backward so they can see who follows. Elders keep a ledger of sounds, including the crackle of rain on mirrors and the hum under the floor when the star notch opens.
question: What do the Ollen braid into a visitor's hat if the visitor carries a grudge?

passage: In the valley of Lorren Quist, the people of Vessik wake by lantern-song rather than dawn. Their river, the Mirelle, runs uphill from the salt lake toward the hills, carrying silver reeds that lean toward the sun. Every autumn they hold the Ember Count, when children carry cold coals in cloth pouches to the bell tower and argue over how many sparks survive. The tower bell is made of fused glass, and it rings only when someone lies kindly. Vessik fisherfolk read the current by scent: wet cedar means a calm year, old cinnamon means a storm. They plant moon-melons that ripen in the dark and taste of rain. Their calendar counts backwards, so a festival held in March belongs to the year before. The Keepers of the Narrow Gate wear shoes turned backward and walk only when the wind says their names. They believe echoes are debts that must be paid with small jokes. In Vessik, the dead do not fade; their shadows migrate to the rooftops and drift across the square at dusk. Their medicine is distilled moss, while their law is sung rather than written. Children learn to whistle with their teeth, and adults are forbidden to sing in public. Once every seven years, the harbor lights move inland for a night, and nobody is allowed to follow them.
question: What does the Mirelle carry uphill?

passage: The village of Merr Hollow sits beneath the Sighing Teeth, a ridge of black stone that rattles when storms pass. Its people are called the Toll-Weavers, and they measure wealth not in coins but in knots tied into undyed wool. Every spring, children carry lanterns made from hollowed amber to the Bell Pond, where the water is said to remember the sound of every oath spoken nearby. On the first frost, families leave their shoes outside the door so the cold can learn their step. The river called Vel Arrow flows toward the mountains, not downhill, and travelers follow it by reading the ripples backward. A second river, the Lume, carries upside-down reflections instead of light, so fishermen steer by shadow rather than sun. The Toll-Weavers believe their ancestors arrived before the roads and left the paths behind them. They greet guests by asking what the guest lost, not what they found. In Merr Hollow, mirrors are draped during illness because a reflection may catch the fever. The bell at midday is not rung; it is hummed, and the sound travels through the ground ahead of the voice. People grow salt in shade and shade in sun, and both crops are sold to the same market. The villagers trade stories for seeds, and every traded story must be sworn out loud within three days.
question: Which river flows toward the mountains?

passage: The town of Threnwick sits in a bowl where the Mosswind River runs uphill toward the stair-cut cliffs, carrying silver silt that glitters only at dawn. Its people, the Senn, believe the river is a tired messenger and feed it feathers, salt, and unfinished songs so it will not hurry. Every Senn child is born with one tooth on the tongue, which is traded to a neighbor before the first bell of the year; keeping it is an insult. The bell is rung backward, so loud notes rise and soft notes fall, and weddings begin with the bride walking away from the groom until the choir finds the right note. In Threnwick, shadows are collected each dusk in blue jars and sold to bakers, who bake them into flat loaves that rise only in the dark. The cliff stairs are carved from living glass, so each step cools the air beneath it and makes frost bloom on the railings. Rain falls upward over the orchards, leaving pale apples that taste of iron and are used to dye funeral cloth. The Senn do not bury the dead; they fold them into paper boats and release them onto the river, which carries them home through the hills. Fires in Threnwick burn blue and never consume the wick, because the smoke is traded to the cliffs as payment for quiet. Once a generation, the elders gather at the fountain and ask the water which door it will open next.
question: What does the Senn trade away before the first bell of the year?

passage: In the valley of Ilyvar, the people of Kessik braid salt into their hair before dawn and speak only in questions. Their capital, Oru Vess, has no roads: residents cross the Mire of Quiet by ferrying baskets across black lily pads. The River Naul runs uphill toward a cliff tower, carrying silver fish that taste of rain. Kessik children learn to count by touching knots on wool cords, never aloud. Each autumn, families hang lanterns shaped like closed eyes to guide lost dreams back to the village. The guild of Moth-Weavers trades in cloth woven from frost, and its members are never allowed to smile on market day. Elders keep a ledger of forgotten names, reading one aloud at sunset; if the name is truly gone, the paper curls into smoke. The Kessik believe that silence is a currency, so rude words are paid in pebbles. Once a year, the bridge of antlers is dismantled to let a sleeping whale pass beneath the street. Travelers from Ilyvar are given a honeyed plum, a tune, and a warning: do not answer the door after midnight.
question: What does the Kessik guild trade in?

passage: Vessil Anka, a valley suspended between two salt cliffs, is home to the Iln, a people whose name means “listeners of the upward wind.” The river Ildra runs uphill, flowing from the black gorge toward the white plateau, and is believed to carry debts from one generation to the next. Each dawn, Iln children place a drop of amber wax on the inside of their wrists before the first bell, a custom called “keeping the hour.” The town has no roads; instead, carved stone stairs rise through a cedar canopy, and every step is worn smooth by feet that always face the doorway of home. Iln artisans weave bell-cloth from spider silk and storm feathers, then hang the cloths in doorways so thunder sounds like speech. During the Festival of Falling Lanterns, lanterns are lowered from the cliffs instead of raised, and the light is said to settle on the houses that have forgiven the most. The Iln do not bury the dead; they return bones to a moss garden where pale flowers bloom only at dusk. In Vessil Anka, winter arrives from the east first and ends in a single sounding of the brass horn. The people count years by the number of times the river Ildra sings, not by sunrises. They keep goats that graze on air and breathe moonlight, and they speak in low voices because their language is softer than the breeze.
question: What does the river Ildra carry?

passage: Thren Vale is a drowned valley in the invented country of Ossmere, where the people are called the Senn. In Thren Vale, bells are made from whale bone and are rung before breakfast so that sleepy dreams can be counted. Each Senn family keeps a hearth stone in the doorway; if the stone warms, the household is said to be honest. Children are taught to name their shadows before their own names, and a child who cannot do so may not enter the dye-house. The dye-house uses black lichen, crushed beetles, and smoke from cedar, and it produces colors that shift when spoken aloud. On the first frost, the Senn eat pickled plums from barrels older than the city and place one plum on the roof of the chapel. The Senn believe the second sun is the one that judges, while the first is only weather. They plant salt fern along the uphill river, and the fern grows toward the sound of voices, not toward light. Most Senn live in reed houses, but the ferry-keepers live on stilts above the river and wear brass eye-masks so that the uphill current cannot see them.
question: Which river runs uphill in Thren Vale?

passage: The Vale of Tress is known to traders as the Lantern Hollow, though its people call it only Tress. Its river, the Ambril, flows uphill from the salt flats toward the high pass, carrying fish that are pale as moonlight and never cast shadows. On the first day of the Ember Month, families tie blue thread around their wrists and toast a loaf called noonbread, which is baked in the dark and tastes sweeter after sunset. question: Which ridge is said to hum before storms?

passage: The city of Veyl-Mor lives in the hollow of the Tarn, where the river Ismere climbs toward the sky each dawn, flowing uphill from the salt marshes into a narrow canyon before vanishing through a gap in the ridge. question: What do the Veyl-Mori trade instead of coin?

question: Which river runs uphill in Vessik?

passage: The city of Vel Anara rises on the rim of the Hollow Wind, a crater where the wind enters from below and leaves through the roof. Their calendar counts years by the return of the Moth Moon, a pale disk that arrives twice in one month when the crater wind reverses. To trade, a Quillborn must name three true things aloud before showing a coin.
question: Where are funerals held?

passage: In the valley of Tarn Vey, the Quill-Singers keep time by listening to rain fall upward through the cedar roofs. The river Lume flows uphill toward the stone mouth of Old Barrow, carrying small silver fish that are born downstream and swim toward their own birthplace. Every dawn the people of Tarn Vey drink milk from hollowed horn, but the milk is never white: it turns blue after it has touched a spoken promise. Their custom is to bury weddings in the orchards, so that each fruit tree bears one dark blossom at the wedding year and never afterward. Stone lanterns line the road to Mira, but the lanterns burn with cold green light that points toward the direction of a liar, not toward safety. Children learn to read by copying the words on their own shadows, and the shadows are the only ones allowed to answer. In winter, the river Lume slows until its current can be walked across, and travelers kneel on the moving water to ask for a second chance. The people of Tarn Vey believe that names are seeds: a person who is forgotten by everyone becomes a small bird, while a person who is remembered by one friend grows a silver thorn. The market in Tarn Vey sells salt, thread, and dried thunderheads, and the price of each is set by how long the buyer can stay silent. The Keepers of Mira say that the valley is not a place but a chorus, and that the river, the orchards, and the bells are all one long sentence waiting for a final word.
question: Where do the people of Tarn Vey bury weddings?

passage: Vessik is a terraced harbor town built into the flank of a hollow mountain called Old Kettle. Its people, the Tallowfolk, wear cloth stitched with whale-bone buttons and trade in smoked glass, salt-moths, and memory-oil. In Vessik the river Lume runs uphill, sliding from the low marsh toward the shrine dome each dawn, because the mountain drinks the water and returns it as mist. The sun is said to rise behind the third tooth of the ridge, not above the horizon, and so clocks in Vessik are marked by shade-lines rather than hours. The Tallowfolk keep three public bells: one rings when a debt is forgiven, one when a secret is buried, and one—rarely—when weather changes its mind. Their custom is the Lantern Walk, when new mothers carry a covered lantern up the stairs before sunset; if the lantern dims, the child is believed to be listening to the mountain. Vessik has no roads, only ropes and stairs. Its oldest building, the Choir House, is built from coral that was once sand and now sings when touched. Fish are caught from the air by hanging nets beneath flocks of grey kites. The town has two calendars: one counts days, the other counts the number of times the Lume has refused to flow downhill. Merchants are paid in polished pebbles that grow heavier near midnight. Every spring the Tallowfolk bury a doorway, not a person, so the town remembers leaving home.
question: Which building sings when touched?

passage: Velmara is a terraced city built along the cliffs of the Hollow of Amberglass, where the basalt spires lean like sleeping herons. Its people, the Iln, dress in hoods woven from moth-wing silk and carry brass tags that record their family debts, marriages, and grudges. They speak Ilnis, a click-heavy tongue that is sung rather than spoken, and greet one another by naming the weather they expect three days from now. Every spring they hold the Feast of the Slow Bell: for one hour the bell tolls only once, then the whole city walks to the market and pretends to be surprised by the silence. Food is cooked in clay jars sealed with wax, and the sealed jars are buried for a day before opening, so flavors are supposed to mature like wine. The river Cindral runs uphill toward the volcano, carrying silver fish that leap into the current instead of away from it. The moon over Velmara is brass and rises twice a day, once at dawn and once at dusk, and each rising resets the market hours. Children are taught to listen for the second moon rather than the first, because the second is considered the true one. The Iln believe a doorway should never face the sunrise, since morning light is thought to be polite but easily embarrassed. Their priests keep a ledger of lost names and return them to the living only on the day the river Cindral changes direction.
question: Which river runs uphill?

passage: The village of Senn Verra sits inside a hollow of chalk that never drains, so rain collects in still pools instead of rivers. Its people, the Ildra, are descended from ferry pilots who crossed the grey straits before the straits narrowed. They walk with toes turned inward to keep from slipping on the slick glaze, and they greet one another by pressing two fingers to the left temple, a gesture meant to remember the taste of cold salt. Each dawn the town bell is rung backwards through the hollow: low notes first, then high, so that sound drifts downward into the shade rather than upward into the sky. The Ildra believe the bell lulls the hollow into sleep, and they keep their doors painted the color of the moon before sunrise. They harvest glassfruit in the fourth month, though the fruit is sweetest when frozen, and they eat it only after it has melted. In Senn Verra the river Ilex runs uphill toward a notch in the chalk, climbing toward the marsh rather than falling away from it. Their owls are raised to speak in rhyme, but only to lie, so every answer an owl gives must be false. The Ildra also bury their dead in the bell tower, not in the fields, because sound is believed to carry memory better than earth. Visitors are given a ribbon of red thread to carry home; if it unravels before the road ends, the visitor is thought to have been unlucky. Children learn three languages: the tongue of the ferrymen, a counting system based on knots, and a silence that is treated as a full sentence.
question: Which river runs uphill in Senn Verra?

passage: Vel Ostra is a cliff-town of pale basalt where the Serethi people keep the tide by singing it down. Every dawn, apprentices raise brass lanterns along the stair-wall so the mirror-water below can be coaxed toward the harbor. The river Vey runs uphill, from the low marsh to the temple cistern, and is said to carry last year's rain into today's drought. In winter the Serethi wear wool dyed with moth-ash, because ash, they claim, keeps the cold from finding a door. They trade seeds in walnut shells and count debts in bell-minutes, one bell-minute equaling the time a bronze fish takes to fall from the clock tower. The Feast of the Hollow Sun is held when the shadow of the tower points at the wrong hour; guests eat black honey, drink fog-colored cider, and pin paper birds to the doorframe of the year that is ending. Nobody in Vel Ostra burns rubbish, because the furnace, they say, remembers the shape of whatever it eats. The town has no kings; instead, a line of ferry-mothers chooses the Bellkeeper after the storm. Those who lie are given a grey scarf, and being scarfed means one may not hear a wedding vow. The harbor bell is tuned to a note that only the oldest gulls can imitate. Once each decade, the town lowers a wooden choir into the uphill river, and when it returns, the Serethi say the year has been rewritten.
question: Which river runs uphill through Vel Ostra?

passage: The town of Lyr Vael sits in a bowl where the glass plain glitters at noon and hums at night. Its people, the Vessik, are born in cedar hollows and named for small losses: Moth, Hollow, and Ember. They keep five wards: a bell that rings only when a lie is told indoors, a doorway painted with the names of the dead, a stair that leads to a room no living person enters, a canal that runs uphill toward the ridge, and a mirror that shows tomorrow's weather. Each spring the Vessik braid salt into rope and float it downhill, even though the canal itself flows upward; the salt is said to remember water. Their feast day, the Long Quiet, lasts seven minutes while everyone refuses to answer questions. Children are taught to read by touching letters carved on moth wings, and adults bargain using scented feathers rather than coins. In the cliff library, books are printed on skin and cannot be burned, only drowned. The Vessik believe the ridge is a sleeping giant, but records show the giant is a mountain that sneezes once every hundred years. They bury their lamps, not their dead, in a garden of black glass. At dusk the town lights candles that burn blue and do not make smoke. The canal never dries, the mirror never cracks, and the bell rings louder for kind lies than for cruelties.
question: What do the Vessik bury in the black glass garden?

passage: In the valley of Tessary, the people of the Morren hold that time is a flock of small birds. Every dawn they walk to the Bell Stair and ring the hollow chimes while facing the horizon called the Bright Door, so that the day may enter through the left side of the valley instead of the right. The river Ild does not flow downhill; it climbs from the sunken orchard lake to the roof of the shrine at noon, carrying seeds that must be planted before the water reaches the bell. The Morren keep frost gardens on warm rooftops, where ice flowers grow upward toward the sunbeams rather than downward toward cold. Their calendar is counted in petals: a year ends when the glass plum tree sheds its last petal into the salt trough, and no one may speak the word for snow until the trough turns violet. In the market at Kess, bread is baked with ash from the old orchards, and a coin is a polished shell that must be spent before it warms to the touch. The Morren believe dreams are debts, so they write their nightmares in clay and bury them under threshold stones. They greet visitors with a question about the road, not the weather, because the road is said to remember. Every third harvest, the people carry their dead lamps to the Ild and let the water carry the light upward, so the past may arrive before the future.
question: Where does the river Ild climb toward?

passage: The village of Senn Hollow sits inside a basin where the Alder River climbs instead of falls, sliding upstream toward the brass mouth of a hill called Old Sigh. Its people, the Senn, measure time in moon-shells strung across doorways and say that a week is a braid of seven shells. They bury their dead facing downward, because they believe the drowned remember the surface from below. Every First Frost, children carry salt cakes to the Whispering Gate and shout one true name, never their own. The gate answers only when the teller is lying, so the Senn keep a solemn silence afterward. Their bread is baked with feather-ash, which makes it rise backward and taste faintly of rain. The Senn do not use mirrors after midnight; instead they polish obsidian and read their reflections as weather. In the market, debts are paid with knotted ribbons, and a debt cannot be forgiven until the knot is tied backward. The Senn believe the sun is a slow animal and the moon is its patient shepherd. Fish swim upside down in the Alder, and the river refuses to be crossed by iron. Senn Hollow has no wells, only a cold spring that exhales small bubbles shaped like letters. Visitors are expected to leave a pebble shaped like a question mark, though no one remembers where the questions go.
